chapter_summary:
A critical skill for any RHEL administrator is the ability to monitor system resources. Proactive monitoring allows you to detect performance bottlenecks, anticipate potential issues like full disks or memory exhaustion, and diagnose problems when they arise. By understanding how to use various command-line tools to check CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network usage, you can ensure your systems remain healthy and perform optimally.

Let's begin with CPU. The `uptime` command provides a quick overview, showing how long the system has been running and, crucially, the load averages for the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Load average represents the average number of processes that are either running or waiting to run. A load average consistently higher than the number of CPU cores often indicates a CPU bottleneck. For a more detailed, real-time view, `top` and `htop` (as discussed in Chapter 5.3) are invaluable. They show per-process CPU usage, total CPU utilization, and other system statistics. High CPU usage by a single process or a consistently high system-wide percentage in `top` suggests a CPU-bound workload. You can also use `sar` (System Activity Reporter, part of the `sysstat` package) for historical data, e.g., `sar -u 5 3` to report CPU utilization every 5 seconds, 3 times.

Memory management is another vital area. The `free -h` command provides a human-readable summary of your system's physical memory (RAM) and swap space. It shows total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory. Understanding the difference between "free" and "available" is important: "free" is truly unused memory, while "available" includes memory that is used by the kernel for caching but can be quickly reclaimed by applications. High "used" memory isn't necessarily bad if "available" memory is still ample. However, if your system is consistently using a lot of swap space (indicated by high "used" in the Swap line), it means your system is running out of physical RAM and is heavily relying on slower disk-based swap, which significantly degrades performance. This is a strong indicator that you need more RAM.

Disk space is a common concern. The `df -h` command reports file system disk space usage in a human-readable format. It shows the total size, used space, available space, and percentage used for each mounted file system. A file system approaching 100% usage can cause applications to fail, prevent log files from being written, and even lead to system instability. It's crucial to monitor these percentages. To find out which directories or files are consuming the most space, the `du -sh /path/to/directory` command (disk usage, summarize, human-readable) is extremely useful. Running `du -sh *` in a problematic directory can quickly pinpoint large subdirectories. Remember that `df` reports block usage, while `du` reports actual file usage, so their numbers might differ slightly.

Beyond just space, disk I/O performance can be a major bottleneck. The `iostat` command (also part of `sysstat`) provides statistics on CPU utilization and I/O statistics for devices and partitions. Running `iostat -x 1` will show extended statistics every second, including `%util` (percentage of time the device was busy), `r/s` (reads per second), `w/s` (writes per second), `rkB/s` (read kilobytes per second), and `wkB/s` (write kilobytes per second). A `%util` consistently close to 100% for a disk indicates that the disk is a bottleneck, and applications are waiting for I/O operations to complete. This could point to slow storage, an inefficient application, or excessive logging.

Network activity is the final piece of the resource monitoring puzzle. The `ss` command (socket statistics) is the modern replacement for `netstat` on RHEL and other Linux systems. It can display information about network sockets, showing active connections, listening ports, and network statistics. For example, `ss -tuln` shows all TCP and UDP listening ports (`-t` for TCP, `-u` for UDP, `-l` for listening, `-n` for numeric addresses). `ss -s` provides a summary of socket statistics. If you suspect network issues, `ss` can help identify open ports, active connections, and potential connection floods. Tools like `ping` and `traceroute` are also essential for basic network connectivity testing.

When interpreting these metrics, always look for trends and baselines. What is "normal" for your system? Spikes in CPU or I/O that quickly resolve might be acceptable, but sustained high usage indicates a problem. Combine information from different tools: high CPU *and* high disk I/O might suggest an application is thrashing (e.g., constantly reading/writing small files). High memory usage *and* high swap usage unequivocally points to memory starvation. Proactive monitoring, setting up alerts, and regularly reviewing these metrics are crucial for maintaining a healthy and performant RHEL environment.

screens.title: Monitoring System Resources
screens.subtitle: Detect performance issues across CPU, memory, disk, I/O, and network using standard Linux tools

narration.text: Monitoring system resources is a core skill for any RHEL administrator because it lets you spot performance problems before users notice them. In this lesson you'll learn how to read load averages from uptime, inspect live C P U and process metrics with top and htop, examine memory and swap details with free, find disk usage with df and du, measure input and output with iostat, and inspect sockets with ss. Each command gives a different vantage point: some show a live snapshot, others record historical trends. I will show concrete command examples, how to interpret the most important fields, and common misconceptions such as confusing free memory with available memory or assuming high disk usage always means an input and output problem. By the end you will be able to combine outputs — for example, correlating high load averages with disk %util — to identify likely bottlenecks quickly. Think of these tools as a diagnostic toolkit: they are lightweight, available on most systems, and together they help you form a clear hypothesis about what to fix. To get practical, we'll run typical commands, examine sample outputs, and practice reading the numbers that matter.

keyIdea.title: Chapter Core
keyIdea.text: Use uptime, top/htop, free, df/du, iostat, and ss to observe system behavior, form baselines, and identify bottlenecks such as CPU saturation, memory exhaustion, full filesystems, high disk %util, or network connection floods.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map directly to the practical monitoring skills you'll practice. First, you'll monitor C P U utilization and interpret load averages with uptime, top, and htop so you can tell when compute demand exceeds available cores. Second, you'll analyze memory with free and read swap usage to detect memory starvation. Third, you'll evaluate disk space and inode use with df and du so you can find large files and containers of many small files. Fourth, you'll monitor disk input and output using iostat to determine when storage devices are busy and causing waits. Each objective includes a short explanation of what success looks like and a small mnemonic to help you recall the command and its intended observation. These are not abstract goals: they are hands-on competencies. By the time you finish the lesson and exercises, you will be able to run the commands, read the key fields, and form a hypothesis about the source of slow behaviour based on those outputs.

narration.text: Beyond knowing commands, success means forming baselines and using multiple metrics together. Objective five is to use sar to collect historical C P U and input and output data so you can confirm whether high load is transient or sustained. Objective six is to track active network connections with ss to detect port floods or unexpected services. Objective seven is to correlate metrics — for example, pairing high load average with disk %util reported by iostat to identify input and output-bound workloads. Objective eight is to interpret outputs and recommend remediation: add R A M when swap is constant, clean logs or archive files when df shows near-100% usage, or investigate processes when top shows sustained high C P U per process. Each of these objectives is practical: you will run commands, interpret their numbers, and write short remediation steps based on those interpretations.

screens.title: Load Average and uptime
screens.subtitle: Understanding the 1, 5, and 15 minute load averages

narration.text: Load average measures the average number of processes that are either running or waiting for C P U and runs over three intervals: 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It is not a percentage; instead, it is a simple count. On a single-core system, a load average of 1.0 means the C P U was fully utilized on average. On a four-core system, a load average of 4.0 likewise means full utilization. A load that consistently exceeds the number of C P U cores indicates more work is queued than the C P U can handle, which is a C P U bottleneck. A practical example: uptime prints load averages quickly. If uptime returns 2.10, 1.80, 1.25 on a two-core VM, that suggests sustained overload because 2.10 exceeds two cores. A common misconception is to equate high load always with C P U-bound work — sometimes processes are blocked waiting on disk input and output but still count in the run queue, inflating load averages. To resolve the cause, pair load average with top or iostat: if iostat shows %util near 100% on a device, the high load may be input and output-bound, not pure C P U saturation. Key takeaway: compare load averages to core count and always correlate with other tools before deciding to add C P U resources.

keyIdea.title: Load Average Meaning
keyIdea.text: Load averages are counts of runnable or waiting processes over time; compare them to CPU core count and correlate with I/O metrics before concluding a CPU problem.

content.html:
Core Concept Load Average
Interpreting uptime and load averages
Relate averages to core count and check for I/O waits before concluding the issue is CPU.
Definition

Load average is the average number of processes runnable or waiting for CPU over 1, 5, and 15 minutes. It counts both running and waiting processes, including those blocked on I/O.

Common misconception

High load does not always mean CPU usage; blocked processes waiting on disk or network also increase the run queue.

Key Takeaway

Always compare load averages to CPU core count and correlate with iostat or top to find the underlying cause.

Example: uptime output
  10:32:14 up 12 days,  3:14,  2 users,  load average: 2.10, 1.80, 1.25
If this system has two CPU cores, a 2.10 1-minute load is a sign of sustained saturation. If iostat shows high %util for disks, the queued processes may be waiting on storage instead.
Check with top
Observe per-process CPU and the CPU% column to see if one process drives the load.
Check with iostat
If disk %util is high, the load may be I/O-bound rather than compute-bound.

screens.title: Using top and htop
screens.subtitle: Inspect per-process CPU and memory usage in real time

narration.text: top and htop provide a live view of processes and resource consumption. top is installed by default and shows a compact view including per-process C P U%, memory usage, and system averages. htop, when available, gives a more readable, interactive view with per-core bars and easier sorting. A practical example: run top and watch the over-time C P U% column to see which processes are consuming C P U. If a single process holds high C P U for several minutes, you likely have a C P U-bound issue. Use the process ID to investigate further. A misconception is to treat a transient spike as a persistent problem; short C P U bursts are common and acceptable. To distinguish transient from sustained issues, sample over time with top or use sar to capture historical data. Another practical tip: in top, look at the load averages at the top and the PID column to map load to a culprit process. If you see many processes in 'D' state (uninterruptible sleep), these are likely waiting on input and output and point away from pure C P U causes. The closing question: when you observe a sustained C P U consumer, do you profile the process, adjust scheduling, or scale resources — and which will be most effective?

keyIdea.title: Live Process View
keyIdea.text: Use top for a default live snapshot and htop for a richer per-core view; correlate long-running high CPU processes with load averages and I/O state to decide remediation.

content.html:
Process Monitoring top & htop
Inspect running processes
Identify high-CPU processes, long-running tasks, and processes waiting on I/O.
Example: top snapshot
top - 10:45:22 up 5 days,  1:22,  2 users,  load average: 3.12, 2.45, 1.80
Tasks: 189 total,   1 running, 188 sleeping,   0 stopped,   0 zombie
%Cpu(s): 92.1 us,  3.7 sy,  0.0 ni,  4.2 id,  0.0 wa,  0.0 hi,  0.0 si,  0.0 st
PID USER      PR  NI    VIRT    RES    SHR S  %CPU %MEM     TIME+ COMMAND
2345 appuser   20   0  1024m 512m  12m R  85.3 10.4   120:34 myapp
Here a single process consumes most CPU. That points to a CPU-bound workload and suggests profiling or scaling across cores.
Pro tip & Common mistake
If many processes show state 'D', they are waiting on kernel I/O and indicate storage issues. Do not immediately add CPUs without checking I/O.
Check with htop
htop visualizes per-core usage and lets you sort by CPU, memory, or runtime to find long-lived high consumers quickly.
Key Takeaway

Use top/htop to identify whether a few processes drive load and check process states to distinguish CPU waits from I/O waits.

screens.title: Understanding free -h and swap
screens.subtitle: Distinguish free, used, buff/cache, and available memory

narration.text: Memory reporting on Linux requires interpretation. free -h prints total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory in a human-friendly format. The crucial difference: free is memory that is completely unused, while available includes memory the kernel is using for filesystem caches that applications can reclaim quickly. So high used memory by itself is not necessarily bad. Swap, by contrast, is disk-backed virtual memory used when R A M is short. If Swap Used grows and stays high, it usually indicates the system is out of physical R A M and is moving pages to disk, which slows performance dramatically. A concrete example: free -h may show 16G total, 14G used, 1G free, but 6G available — meaning the system caches much of the used memory and can return it when needed. A common misconception is to add R A M immediately when used is high; instead, check available and swap to see if the kernel can reclaim memory. If swap is persistently high, add R A M or reduce memory footprint. Practical steps include identifying which processes use the most memory with top and considering tuning application memory or adding swap only as a temporary measure. How would you act if swap is near full but available remains low? That pattern signals urgent need for more R A M or memory optimization.

keyIdea.title: Memory vs Swap
keyIdea.text: Interpret free -h carefully: available is what matters for new allocations; sustained swap use is a clear sign of insufficient physical RAM.

content.html:
Memory Monitoring free -h & Swap
Read memory values correctly
Focus on available memory and swap used to assess true memory pressure.
Example output
              total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           16G         14G        1.0G        200M        1.0G         6G
Swap:          8.0G        4.0G        4.0G
Despite 14G used, 6G available means cache can be reclaimed. Swap used at 4G is a warning: physical RAM has been exhausted earlier.
Decision points
  • If available is healthy, no immediate action.
  • If swap is high and remains so, add RAM or reduce app memory.
  • Use top to find memory-hungry processes and consider tuning them.
Common mistake
Treating 'used' as the only metric — kernel cache can make used look large even when memory is available.
Key Takeaway

Look at available and swap together; persistent swap activity means the system is starved for RAM.

screens.title: df -h vs du -sh and inodes
screens.subtitle: Block usage, file usage, and inode exhaustion explained

narration.text: Disk reporting has two complementary views. df -h reports filesystem block usage per mount point: total, used, available, and percentage used. du -sh reports the disk usage of a directory and sums files within it. Because df reports blocks and du sums file sizes, their numbers can differ slightly, especially with sparse files or deleted-but-open files. Inodes are another resource to monitor: each file and directory consumes an inode. A filesystem can run out of inodes even when there is free block space, preventing new files from being created. A concrete example: df -h / may show 20% usage while df -i / shows 100% inode usage; the cause is many small files. Use du -sh /var/log to find large directories and use find to count files when suspecting inode exhaustion. Common misconceptions include assuming low percent use in df means no problems; inode exhaustion is invisible to df -h. Key actions: run df -i to check inodes, use du -sh * in an offending directory to find large subdirectories, and consider removing or archiving many small files or changing the filesystem layout when inodes are repeatedly exhausted. The closing reflective question: when you face inode exhaustion, will you clean up, change the application, or reprovision with a filesystem configured with more inodes?

keyIdea.title: Space vs Inodes
keyIdea.text: df reports block usage, du reports actual directory usage, and df -i reveals inode consumption; run all three to diagnose file-creation issues.

content.html:
Disk Space df vs du & Inodes
Blocks, files, and inodes
Use df, du, and df -i together to find both large files and inode exhaustion.
Example commands
# Check block usage
$ df -h /
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        50G   10G   37G  22% /

# Check inode usage
$ df -i /
Filesystem     Inodes  IUsed   IFree IUse% Mounted on
/dev/sda1      3276800 3276800 0     100% /

# Find large dirs
$ sudo du -sh /var/log
2.6G    /var/log
Practical guidance
  • Use df -h for overall space; use du -sh to locate large subtrees.
  • Run df -i when users report inability to create files despite free space.
  • Remove or rotate logs and consider filesystem reformat only when necessary.
Common Mistake

Assuming df -h alone is sufficient; it will not reveal inode exhaustion which prevents file creation.

screens.title: Measuring disk I/O with iostat
screens.subtitle: Interpreting %util, r/s, w/s, and throughput metrics

narration.text: iostat provides device-level input and output statistics that help you determine whether storage is the bottleneck. With the sysstat package installed, running iostat -x 1 shows extended stats every second. Important columns include r/s and w/s for read and write operations per second, rkB/s and wkB/s for throughput, and %util for the percentage of time the device was busy. A sustained %util near 100% indicates the device is continuously busy and likely the bottleneck. For example, if iostat shows %util 98, high w/s, and long await times, processes may be waiting on writes and overall response will be slow. A common misconception is to treat high throughput alone as bad; high throughput with low %util means the device handles the load well. Conversely, high %util with modest throughput indicates the device is saturated, possibly because of small input and output sizes or high IOPS demands. Use iostat together with top: if many processes are in uninterruptible sleep and iostat shows high %util, storage is the likely culprit. Key actions include moving heavy workloads to faster storage, tuning application input and output patterns, or reducing logging intensity. Which remediation fits depends on whether the bottleneck is device speed, IOPS, or application behavior.

keyIdea.title: I/O Bottlenecks
keyIdea.text: Use iostat -x to spot disks with high %util and long await times; correlate with process states to confirm I/O-bound workloads.

content.html:
Disk I/O iostat -x
Assess device utilization
Look for %util near 100% and long await times to identify saturated storage.
Sample iostat -x 1 output
Device            r/s    w/s   rkB/s  wkB/s  await  %util
sda               5.0   40.0  1024.0 8192.0 35.2   98.3
sdb               0.1    0.2    10.0   12.0  2.1    1.2
Here sda is nearly saturated at 98% util with high await; sdb is mostly idle. This suggests moving workload off sda or investigating high-write behavior.
Interpretation checklist
  • %util ~100% → device busy, probable I/O bottleneck.
  • High await → long I/O latency, user-facing slowdown likely.
  • High w/s with low %util → device handles throughput well; check IOPS vs block size.
Pro Tip

Sample repeatedly and compare devices; one busy disk can dominate a server's performance even if others are idle.

screens.title: Using ss to inspect sockets
screens.subtitle: List listeners, active connections, and socket summaries

narration.text: ss replaces netstat as the modern tool for listing sockets and connections. Use ss -tuln to show TCP and UDP listening sockets with numeric addresses and ports; ss -s gives a compact socket summary. These commands help you detect unexpected listening services, connection floods, or large numbers of established connections that may overload the network stack or the application. For example, ss -tuln may reveal an unexpected process bound on a high port that should not be exposed, while ss -s can show you totals for TCP: established, closed, orphaned, and timed-wait sockets. A common misconception is to assume network slowness is always external; internal connection floods or too many simultaneous connections can saturate a server. When you see many established connections, check the listening service and consider rate-limiting, connection pooling, or load balancing. Combine ss with top and iostat: a service with many connections and high C P U suggests the application, while many connections with low C P U but high disk input and output may point to backend storage issues. The takeaway: ss helps you find anomalies in the socket landscape quickly so you can act on security or performance issues.

keyIdea.title: Socket Inspection
keyIdea.text: Use ss -tuln to find listeners and ss -s for socket totals; identify connection floods or unexpected services and correlate with application load.

content.html:
Network Monitoring ss
Inspect listeners and connections
Quickly surface listening ports and socket counts that affect service health and security.
Example commands and output
$ ss -tuln
Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port
tcp   LISTEN 0      128    0.0.0.0:22        0.0.0.0:*
udp   UNCONN 0      0      0.0.0.0:123       0.0.0.0:*

$ ss -s
Total: 123 (kernel: 100)
TCP:   20 (estab 10, closed 5, orphaned 0, timewait 5)
If established connections are unexpectedly high, the service or clients may be misbehaving or under a flood attack.
Checklist
  • Run ss -tuln to list listening sockets and validate expected services.
  • Run ss -s to see totals and watch for unusual counts like many timewait sockets.
  • Correlate with application logs to identify client-side issues or attacks.
Warning

Large numbers of sockets in TIME-WAIT or ESTABLISHED can indicate load or connection churn; investigate before scaling horizontally.

screens.title: Using sar for trend analysis
screens.subtitle: Capture CPU and I/O metrics over time to separate spikes from patterns

narration.text: sar, part of the sysstat package, collects and reports historical system activity including C P U and input and output. It is useful when you need to know whether a spike was a one-off or part of a longer pattern. For example, sar -u 5 3 reports C P U utilization every five seconds, three times; configured cron-style collection allows you to review hours or days of data. A concrete scenario: users report occasional slow response around 3am. sar can show whether that time consistently has higher C P U or input and output, indicating a scheduled job. A common misconception is to rely solely on live tools; those only show the current state and can miss intermittent patterns. Another practical point: sar can export metrics into CSV-like formats for longer-term analysis. Use sar together with iostat outputs to confirm that periods of high load correspond to high %util on storage devices. The final takeaway is to build baselines: understand what a normal day looks like so you can spot anomalies; sar is the tool that helps you move from reactive snapshots to proactive trend-based decisions.

keyIdea.title: Historical Metrics
keyIdea.text: Use sar to record and review historical CPU and I/O metrics, enabling you to detect recurring patterns and scheduled workload effects.

content.html:
Historical Analysis sar
Spot recurring patterns and scheduled jobs
Collect data over time to decide whether spikes are transient or systemic.
Example usage
# Report CPU every 5 seconds, 3 times
$ sar -u 5 3
# Use recorded data from /var/log/sa for daily trends
$ sar -f /var/log/sa/sa10 -u
Look for repeated patterns at the same hour across days to identify cron jobs or backups causing load.
Workflow
  1. Enable sysstat collection if not present.
  2. Collect metrics during suspected problem windows.
  3. Compare sar output across days to find consistent spikes.
Key Takeaway

Use sar to turn single snapshots into trend analysis and avoid misdiagnosing transient spikes as persistent problems.

screens.title: Correlating metrics to find bottlenecks
screens.subtitle: Combine CPU, memory, disk, and network signals to form a hypothesis

narration.text: Effective diagnosis comes from correlating measurements across subsystems. A single high metric rarely tells the whole story. For example, a high load average with many processes in 'D' state and high disk %util points to storage input and output as the root cause rather than C P U. Similarly, high C P U with low disk and normal swap suggests compute-bound work. Look for the following patterns: high swap plus low available memory equals memory starvation; high %util on a disk plus long await times indicates an input and output bottleneck; many established sockets tied to a single process plus increased C P U indicates an application under heavy request volume. A concrete scenario: a web server shows slow responses. You run top and see moderate C P U, free -h shows heavy swap, and iostat shows high %util on the log filesystem. The hypothesis is memory pressure causing paging and increased disk writes. The common mistake is acting on a single metric alone. Build a checklist: observe load averages, check top for process states, run free -h for swap, run iostat for device utilization, and use ss for socket counts. Conclude with a remediation plan based on the dominant signal. What combined evidence would convince you to add R A M versus optimize input and output?

keyIdea.title: Correlation Rules
keyIdea.text: Cross-check load, process states, memory, I/O, and sockets to identify the subsystem causing the bottleneck before taking corrective action.

content.html:
Correlation Finding Bottlenecks
Synthesize signals to form a single hypothesis
Use a checklist approach: load → processes → memory → I/O → network.
Checklist
  1. Read load averages from uptime.
  2. Inspect process states with top/htop.
  3. Check memory and swap with free -h.
  4. Check device %util with iostat.
  5. Inspect sockets with ss.
Scenario walk-through
If uptime shows high load, top shows many 'D' states, and iostat shows %util near 100%, the most likely root cause is slow storage. If uptime shows high load and top shows one process with very high CPU% and low iostat %util, the issue is CPU-bound and you should profile the process or scale compute.
Key Takeaway

Always combine metrics to form a diagnosis; single metrics are often misleading without context.

screens.title: Practical command checklist
screens.subtitle: Run these commands to collect the essential snapshot

narration.text: When you need a quick diagnostic snapshot, run a short checklist of commands to capture C P U, memory, disk, input and output, and network state. Start with uptime to read load averages and then run top to spot any obvious process culprits. Run free -h to inspect available memory and swap usage. Use df -h and df -i to check space and inodes, and du -sh on suspect directories to find large consumers. If sysstat is installed, run iostat -x 2 3 to sample device utilization and spot saturated disks. For sockets, run ss -tuln and ss -s to enumerate listening services and totals. A concrete example workflow is: uptime; top -b -n1 to produce a one-shot top; free -h; df -h /; df -i /; sudo du -sh /var/log; sudo iostat -x 2 3; ss -tuln; ss -s. A common mistake is to run these commands but not save output for later comparison — save them or pipe to files. After collecting, compare numbers against your baseline to decide if the values are abnormal. The closing question: after collecting this snapshot, what two metrics would you examine first to decide if the problem is C P U, memory, or input and output related?

keyIdea.title: Snapshot Checklist

screens.title: Interpreting common outputs and assessments
screens.subtitle: Sample questions and reasoning for diagnosing issues

narration.text: Diagnosing is as much about reasoning from evidence as running commands. Consider the assessment question in the chapter: high swap used consistently most likely indicates the system is out of physical R A M. Your reasoning should go: free -h shows swap used at 8GB, available is low, and top shows memory-heavy processes — so swap growth points to R A M shortage. Another assessment: inability to create files despite df -h showing space available suggests inode exhaustion; check df -i to confirm. In practical troubleshooting, always state your evidence and the hypothesis it supports. For example, slow application response: evidence shows load averages > cores, many processes in 'R' or 'D', iostat shows %util near 100 on the data disk, and free -h shows small swap — the most likely hypothesis is input and output-bound behavior. A common mistake here is to recommend a fix such as adding C P U or R A M without matching the dominant signal. Your assessment should include the recommended immediate remediation and a follow-up plan to prevent recurrence: collect sar data, set up monitoring thresholds, and schedule clean-ups or hardware upgrades as needed. The closing question: when faced with limited information, what minimal set of commands would you run to decide the most likely subsystem to fix?

keyIdea.title: Evidence-Based Diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Form hypotheses from multiple command outputs, explain why the evidence supports the conclusion, and list a remediation plus monitoring follow-up.

content.html:
Assessment Reasoning & Diagnosis
Translate outputs into actions
State the evidence, the hypothesis it supports, and your remediation and follow-up plan.
Example assessments
High Swap
Evidence: free -h shows large swap used, available low. Hypothesis: RAM shortage. Fix: increase RAM or reduce app memory; follow up with monitoring and memory profiling.
Cannot create files
Evidence: df -h shows free blocks, but df -i shows 100% inode usage. Hypothesis: inode exhaustion. Fix: delete many small files or reformat with more inodes; follow up with cleanup automation.
Key Takeaway

Assessment requires listing evidence, proposing a hypothesis, and giving a remediation plus a monitoring or prevention plan.

narration.text: These core terms appear throughout monitoring tasks. Load average is the average number of runnable or waiting processes over 1, 5, and 15 minutes; always compare it to C P U core count. Swap space is disk-backed virtual memory used when R A M is insufficient; persistent swap use signals memory shortage. An inode is a filesystem structure that tracks file metadata; running out of inodes prevents new files even when blocks are free. Keep these definitions in mind as you read command outputs so you interpret numbers correctly and avoid common misdiagnoses. Ask yourself: does the number indicate immediate shortage, or is it reclaimable cache? That question will guide whether you clean files, add R A M, or tune application input and output. Module 6 › Key Concepts
Load Average
Average number of runnable or waiting processes over 1, 5, 15 minutes; compare to core count.
Swap Space
Disk-backed virtual memory; heavy, sustained use indicates physical RAM is insufficient.
Inode
Filesystem entry that stores metadata for files and directories; running out of inodes prevents new file creation.
Summary

Remember these basic concepts to interpret monitoring outputs correctly and choose the right remediation path.

screens.title: What to Remember — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Commands and diagnostic signals to keep in mind

narration.text: Keep a short mental checklist of commands and the signals they reveal. Use top/htop for per-process C P U and memory; uptime for quick load averages; free -h for memory and swap status; df -h and du -sh to find space use; iostat -x to detect device saturation with %util; and ss -tuln and ss -s to inspect sockets. When you see a signal, ask which subsystem it implicates and then gather supporting evidence from two other tools. For example, if %util is high in iostat and many processes are in 'D' state, storage is likely at fault. This disciplined, evidence-based approach prevents misdiagnosis and leads to more effective, targeted remediation. What to Remember — Part 2 means top, uptime, free, df, du, iostat, sar, and ss are the core commands; use them in combination and always validate one signal with another.. keyIdea.title: Commands to Use
keyIdea.text: Top, uptime, free, df, du, iostat, sar, and ss are the core commands; use them in combination and always validate one signal with another.

content.html:
Disk I/O
iostat %util near 100% signals a device bottleneck requiring storage tuning or migration.
ss
ss -tuln and ss -s reveal listening services and socket totals to detect floods or unexpected exposure.
sar
Use sar for historical trends and baselines so you can distinguish transient spikes from recurring load.
Final Takeaway

Combine these commands into a short diagnostic workflow, validate signals across tools, and build baselines so you can diagnose and remediate resource bottlenecks confidently.
